To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the luminescence and color of crystals of certain transition-metal complexes change dramatically when ground in an agate mortar.
grinding of crystals of certain gold, platinum, vanadium, and other transition-metal-containing compounds results in changes in the emission spectra of the compounds.

1) the grinding of crystals of certain gold, platinum, or vanadium complexes results in the formation of a new crystal form with different luminescence properties; 2) the grinding of the new crystal form results in the formation a new crystal form; 3) the grinding of this new crystal form results the formation of the original crystal form; and 4) this process is reversible.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the synthesis, structure, and properties of coordination compounds, especially those containing gold and platinum, as well as with the development of methods for the detection of these compounds and their precursors.
the development of new luminescent materials for applications in the field of chemical sensing.
the synthesis, characterization, and reactivity of transition metal complexes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the grinding-induced luminescence change is due to the mechanochemical activation and/or transformation of the crystals.
grinding the crystals results in a change of color and emission wavelength of the crystals.
grinding is a very powerful tool for inducing chemical and structural transformations in the crystal state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that grinding can induce dramatic changes in the luminecence of certain crystalline compounds.
the grinding of crystals of transition-metal complexes is a useful tool for the generation of novel luminescent compounds.
the luminescent properties of transition metal complexes are not always as robust as we might like.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mechanochemical reactions can be used to control the emission color of luminescent crystals.
mechanochemical reactions can be monitored visually by luminescence, a feature that can be used to optimize the reaction conditions and to identify intermediates.
grinding can be a useful way to control luminescence in crystals, and that this approach may be useful in the design of materials for sensing and imaging.
